articles.title: The public absolutely killed it in Week 1
articles.dek: The most-bet sides by money went five for five. Fading the public has been dead for a while — and the receipts from opening weekend explain why people can't stop trying anyway.
articles.author: Fade Desk
articles.sources: Game results via ESPN box scores and team sites. Splits and trader quotes via FOX Sports' Week 1 betting recap and pre-game report, CBS Sports' Week 1 betting guide, Yahoo Sports, VSiN and BetMGM News; the composite most-bet lists as circulated in sportsbook splits reports, with individual entries corroborated by BetMGM, DraftKings and Caesars data. The fade-the-public record via Levitt (The Economic Journal, 2004), the Las Vegas Review-Journal's 2022 bookmaker survey, Flutter and DraftKings earnings disclosures, Nevada Gaming Control Board figures as reported by ESPN, and Sports Insights' published backtests.
body: Twenty of the twenty-four games involving Top 25 programs closed with spreads of twenty points or more — and the big favorites delivered. The most-bet sides by tickets went 3–2. The most-bet sides by money went 5–0.

The fade-the-public gospel says this cannot keep happening. The receipts say otherwise: bookmakers themselves call the balanced-book theory 'an urban legend,' and the 2024 NFL season — 'the most customer friendly since the launch of online sports betting,' by FanDuel's own accounting — cost the industry hundreds of millions.
The real signal this weekend was not the tickets. It was the money — and the prices that moved with it.

mag.coverSub: Opening weekend belonged to the chalk — and the money went undefeated.

quote.text: That extra play and successful Hail Mary was a massive swing for the book. We went from a big winner to a loser.
quote.attr: Adair Horne, BetMGM trading manager, on Michigan's 13–12 escape

sections.title: The Card
sections.headline: Two Lists, One Lesson
sections.sub: The most-bet sides of opening weekend, graded
paras: Every splits report tells two stories: what the crowd bet (tickets) and what the crowd staked (money). In Week 1 they disagreed — and the money was right everywhere. The most-popular sides by ticket count went three-and-two, sunk by Indiana laying forty and a half and an Oregon team that let Boise State hang around. The most-bet sides by dollars went five for five, and the fifth entry was not chalk at all: North Texas, catching that same forty and a half in Bloomington, covered by four and a half points.

The lists are not folklore. At BetMGM, LSU was the most-bet team of the entire Saturday slate by both tickets and money, and cashed by forty-one. At DraftKings, Alabama drew ninety percent of the tickets and ninety-two percent of the handle and covered by ten and a half. Notre Dame, laying twenty and a half at Lambeau, was the most popular bet on the Sunday board and won the second half 28–3 to cover by a touchdown.

figures.label: Most-bet by tickets
figures.note: Won by 41, 38 and 28; Indiana won by 36 and missed, Oregon won by 7 and missed.

figures.label: Most-bet by money
figures.note: Texas covered by 22 and a half. And the one underdog on the list — North Texas, against the ticket-list favorite — covered too.

sections.title: The Weekend
sections.headline: Chalk, Delivered
sections.sub: How the books actually lost it
paras: The slate was built for it: twenty of the twenty-four games involving Top 25 programs closed with spreads of twenty points or more, eleven of them thirty or more. The big brands delivered in big ways — LSU by forty-one in Lane Kiffin's debut, Texas by fifty-two, Alabama by thirty-eight — and, in the words of FOX's weekend recap, customers found success with "pretty much every other big favorite easily covering."

Then there was Michigan. A twenty-seven-and-a-half-point favorite over Western Michigan, trailing 12–6 in the final second, granted a do-over when officials put one second back on the clock — and Bryce Underwood threw a Hail Mary touchdown to win 13–12. Nobody near the spread cared; the moneyline parlays did. BetMGM had taken six times more moneyline bets on Michigan than its opponent, most of them parlay legs, and the replayed snap flipped the book's result on the game. One bettor at Fanatics had put ten thousand dollars on Michigan live at 28-to-1 when the loss looked sealed; the do-over paid $290,000. At Hard Rock, a $1.06 twenty-leg parlay cashed for $130,000.

For balance, the books took Thursday: Washington, Georgia Tech and Auburn — the most public sides of the opening slate — all failed to cover, Georgia Tech losing outright on a last-minute touchdown and a blocked field goal. Readers of this desk will recognize that side. It headlined a certain 2–8 card.

sections.title: The Myth
sections.headline: Nobody Is Balancing the Book
sections.sub: Where fade-the-public came from, and why it died
paras: The fade rests on a folk model: books balance action, shade lines toward the crowd, and profit on the vig — so the other side holds value. The first half is simply false, and bookmakers say so themselves. Asked in 2022 whether books balance bets to lock in profit, the Westgate's Jay Kornegay called the idea "an urban legend." Red Rock's Chuck Esposito: "somewhat of a myth." The South Point's Chris Andrews: "rarely the reality."

The respectable core of the fade was real once. The economist Steven Levitt showed in 2004 that books deliberately carry lopsided positions and price against bettor biases, boosting profits an estimated twenty to thirty percent over a balanced book — and in that era, extreme contrarian positions backtested profitably. But the edge assumed slow, soft lines. Modern prices are set by market-makers and moved by sharp money, not ticket counts; the crowd's tickets barely bend the number. What is left to fade is mostly nothing: over the long run the public wins roughly forty-eight percent of its spread bets — a coin flip minus the price, not an ATM.

sections.title: The Precedent
sections.headline: The Public Has Done This Before
sections.sub: When the crowd breaks the industry
paras: A public weekend is not even unusual anymore. In October 2021, NFL favorites ran the table on an early slate and Caesars' head of trading described it in two words: "a bloodbath." The 2024 NFL season went further — FanDuel's parent called it "the most customer friendly since the launch of online sports betting, with the highest rate of favourites winning in nearly 20 years," and warned of a $370 million revenue hit. DraftKings cut guidance by a quarter-billion. Nevada's books lost money on football in December 2024 — the first losing football month in twelve years.

And here is the other half of the ledger, the reason the books keep the lights on: even in that disaster year, the American industry held 9.3 percent of everything wagered, on record revenue of $13.7 billion. The public wins weekends. The hold wins years. Both of those facts were on display this weekend, and neither one is a betting strategy.

sections.title: The Signal
sections.headline: Watch the Money, Not the Crowd
paras: The week's real tell was the divergence. Indiana drew one-way ticket action at forty and a half — "They're laying the 40 points," Caesars' football trader said — yet the price got bought back toward thirty-nine and a half. The line moved against the tickets, and the tickets lost. In Buffalo's opener, sixty-nine percent of tickets took the Bulldogs while eighty-two percent of the money took Albany; the spread collapsed from twenty-four and a half to eighteen and a half. When tickets and dollars disagree, the dollars are usually somebody who knows something.

Even that is not a system. The only published backtest of fading heavy money in college football found an edge — fifty-five percent — but only in the games where the line moved with the money; where the price stood still, the signal vanished. The splits themselves come from a single recreational book's customers, a keyhole view of a market whose sharpest money never appears in them. The lesson of Week 1 is not that the public is sharp now, or that the fade is back. It is older and simpler: crowds are noise, prices are information, and people are records. The desk grades the people.

call.title: The fade is dead.
call.note: Long live the fade — of the right people. The public is not an ATM, and never was. Records are. That is what the case files are for.

articles.title: Stanford Steve: GameDay's best picker
articles.dek: Twelve years of tracked picks. 648–529 against the spread. Plus 60 units. The numbers say the man beside the headgear is the sharpest voice on the set — with one glaring exception.

sections.title: The Ledger
sections.headline: A Career, Written Down
paras: Every Saturday morning, Steve Coughlin — Stanford Steve to anyone with a television — sits at the College GameDay desk and gives out numbers. Unlike most people who do that for a living, his have been written down. All of them, for twelve years.

Cole's Gameday Blog has tracked every public pick Coughlin has made since 2014 — GameDay, ESPN's betting shows, SportsCenter, all of it. The ledger reads 648 wins, 529 losses and 24 pushes against the spread: 55.1 percent over 1,201 picks, which at standard pricing works out to more than 60 units of profit. The break-even line for a bettor paying −110 is 52.4 percent. Holding three points above it for over a decade is not variance. It is a career.

Among every analyst the site has tracked to a thousand or more picks, no one matches his win rate. Only one picker on the entire board has banked more total units, and it took him three times the volume to do it. The peaks are real, too: a 57–29 season in 2018 worth nearly 23 units, a 53–30 debut in 2014, and a 63–50 start to the current season that already sits 7.4 units in the black.

sections.title: The Asterisk
sections.headline: Mortal on Sundays
sections.sub: The same ledger, the other sport
paras: The receipts cut both ways, and this is where they cut. On NFL Sundays, Stanford Steve is mortal: 166 wins, 162 losses, seven pushes — under 51 percent, eleven units in the red. The same man who prints money on college football gives a share of it back on the professional game.

The gap is the story. Nothing about his process changes between Saturday and Sunday; the market does. College football still leaves room for a person who watches everything to beat the number. The NFL, the most efficient betting market on earth, mostly does not — even for the best picker on the set.

figure.caption: Win percentage against the spread, 2014–2026, as tracked by Cole's Gameday Blog. The rule marks break-even at standard −110 pricing.

sections.title: The Verdict
sections.headline: Context Is the Edge
paras: This is the thesis of Fade in one human being. Records are real. Context is everything. Knowing who is actually good — on which sport, in which spot — is the entire edge, and it only exists because somebody wrote the picks down.
When the GameDay board drops on Saturday, you will know exactly what his number is worth. On Sunday, you will know that too.

call.title: Tail him.
call.note: Fifty-five percent for twelve years on the college game; under fifty-one on the pro one. The record earns the tail — the calendar decides when.

articles.title: LSU is betting on themselves — literally
articles.dek: Five Kalshi block trades, $662,050 down, up to $3 million back — rung for rung, the exact shape of Lane Kiffin's playoff bonus ladder. The school's insurer is holding tickets on the season.
articles.author: Fade Desk
articles.sources: The Athletic (The New York Times), CBS Sports and InGame — reporting on Game Point Capital's Kalshi block trades tied to Lane Kiffin's LSU bonuses, September 2026.

mag.edition: An edition on the business of the game
mag.coverLine: The school is holding tickets on its own season.
mag.coverSub: Five block trades, priced to the dollar of the coach's bonus ladder.

quote.text: Heads, LSU wins. Tails, the market pays.

sections.title: The Bonus
sections.headline: A Ladder Worth Three Million
sections.sub: What LSU owes Lane Kiffin for winning
paras: Lane Kiffin's LSU contract pays him bonuses that climb with every step of a playoff run — $750,000 for getting the Tigers into the College Football Playoff, scaling to $3 million if he wins the national championship. Somebody is on the hook for that money the moment the confetti falls.

Historically, that somebody buys insurance. Schools lay off the risk of their coach's success the way airlines lay off fuel prices — through specialist underwriters, most famously at Lloyd's of London. What changed this month is where the hedge showed up: in public, on an exchange, at prices anyone can look up.

sections.title: The Trade
sections.headline: Five Rungs, One Position
paras: Two weeks before the reports surfaced, five block trades — large positions negotiated off-exchange — hit the prediction market Kalshi, every one of them on LSU's season. The cost of the position was $662,050. The maximum payout, if the Tigers run the table, is $3 million. That is not a round number by accident; it is, to the dollar, Kiffin's championship bonus.

The trades trace to Game Point Capital, a sports insurance firm whose business is protecting schools from the happy disaster of a coach hitting his incentives. Kalshi's chief executive announced a partnership with the firm in February. Similar third-party positions appeared on South Carolina's season a month earlier.

The arithmetic on the first rung shows the machinery plainly: if LSU makes the playoff, the position pays $837,500 — more than covering the $750,000 check the school owes its coach for getting there. Every deeper run pays more, exactly as the obligation grows.

sections.title: The Machine
sections.headline: Infrastructure, Not a Sweat
paras: This is the part of the story a pre-bet desk exists for. Betting markets are no longer just where fans sweat — they are infrastructure. A university's insurance company is functionally long LSU football, in public, at prices you can check between classes. The same markets you can trade are now settling coach bonuses.
So when you watch LSU this season, know that you are not the only one with a position. The school's own hedge is riding every snap — and the money's lean is visible before you make your own call.

articles.title: College football's biggest loser: Clay Travis opens the season 2–8
articles.dek: Eleven public picks. Two winners. A half-point bad beat. Six units gone, one bet still alive tonight — and fifteen seasons of receipts saying none of this is new.
articles.author: Fade Desk
articles.sources: Game results via ESPN box scores and team sites. The Week 1 card as published by Hard Rock Bet ('11 Winners Starting Thursday Night') and tracked by @ExposingClay on X. Season records as stated in Travis's own OutKick columns; fade ledgers via Eleven Warriors ('Slay Travis,' 2017) and The Daily Gopher ('Fade Clay Travis,' 2024–25); the 2019 streak via TheLines. Quotes verbatim from his posts on X, dated.

mag.edition: An edition on getting it wrong in public
mag.coverSub: Clay Travis opened the season 2–8 against the number.

quote.text: I've dug myself an early hole, but as every gambler knows, the only way out of a hole is to keep digging.

sections.title: The Collapse
sections.headline: A Week in Free Fall
sections.sub: He posts the card himself. Graded, it only goes one way.
paras: Every autumn it happens on schedule: Clay Travis publishes his college football card for the world to see, and a measurable share of the internet does the profitable thing — the exact opposite. This is, by his own count, his fifteenth consecutive season of public picks, a run that began in 2011. The first week of the 2026 edition will enter the canon.

Eleven picks went up before Thursday's kickoff — eleven 'winners,' as the column that carries them promised. By Sunday night, eight had lost, and mostly not narrowly. The four long underdogs he asked only to keep things respectable — Stanford, Texas State, Furman, Northern Illinois — lost their games by 39, 52, 47 and 40 points. Clemson, catching ten and a half at LSU, lost Lane Kiffin's debut by 41. The Baylor–Auburn over needed 59 points; the teams produced 33.

Two picks survived: UCLA laying a point and a half at California, which won by three touchdowns, and the Louisville–Ole Miss over, which cashed on a 48-yard field goal as time expired. Graded at one unit per play, the week closed at minus six and two-tenths units — with one bet, Florida State catching three, still alive on Monday night.

figure.label: The week, in units
figure.caption: Cumulative result of the Week 1 card at one unit per play, standard −110 pricing, in the order published. Florida State, still pending, is not charted.

sections.title: The Card
sections.headline: Eleven Picks, Two Winners
sections.sub: Week one, 2026 · As published before kickoff
paras: The card, as published in his Week 1 column and graded at the posted numbers. Read it top to bottom and the shape of the week is unmistakable: seven straight losses before the first winner, and a slate built on long underdogs and high totals — bets that look brave on Thursday and expensive by Saturday night.

The cruelty is in the margins. Georgia Tech, laying six and a half against Colorado, lost outright — a touchdown pass with forty-two seconds left, then a blocked field goal on the final play. And Furman, catching forty-six and a half at Tennessee, lost 56–9: a forty-seven-point margin. The cover died by half a point. It was the closest he came to a third winner all week.

figure.label: The official card
figure.note: He lost Furman +46.5 by a single half point — Tennessee won by forty-seven. It was the closest he came to a third winner all week.

sections.title: The Body of Work
sections.headline: It Was Not the First
paras: The record has a literature. In 2017, the Ohio State site Eleven Warriors spent a full season betting ten dollars against every pick he published and finished 83–67 on the fade — a fourteen percent profit, chronicled week by week and toasted by Deadspin. In 2024 and again in 2025, the Minnesota blog The Daily Gopher ran the same experiment, finished 96–80 and then 94–87 betting the opposite, and donated the winnings to charity. Three season-long fades, three profits.

His own columns tell the same story in the first person. The 2024 season, by his own running count, went from 'a disastrous first two months' at 54–71, to 74–90 at Thanksgiving, to 92–111 by the night of the title game. Last season he stood 82–82 in late November before a three-and-nine week erased the year's work. And in 2019, on Fox's own daily gambling show, he opened with thirteen consecutive losing picks.

He knows. 'My college football picks have been such a disaster this year, you may be better off fading all my picks this week,' he posted in November 2024 — and three weeks later captioned a card, 'So feel free to take the opposite.' At OutKick, his betting show with the Vegas handicapper Kelly Stewart was titled, with no apparent irony, The Fade.

Against all of this stands his own assessment: a claim, made on air, of winning sixty percent of his college bets across a three-year stretch. The handicapper-watchdog site CapperReviews noted that no documented professional has held sixty percent over any three-year period, and publicly challenged him to produce the ledger. The ledger has not appeared.

figure.label: And it was not the first
figure.caption: Win percentage on publicly posted college football picks. 2017 inverted from Eleven Warriors' fade record; 2024–25 as stated in Travis's own columns. The rule marks .500 — break-even before the price.

sections.title: The House
sections.headline: The House Publishes His Picks
paras: None of this has been bad for business. Travis left OutKick in June and launched a new media company, Sport & State, in August — with Hard Rock Bet as an equity investor and its exclusive sportsbook partner. His Week 1 card ran on the sportsbook's own site, under the headline '11 Winners Starting Thursday Night.'

Sit with the mechanics of that: a sportsbook part-owns the company whose founder publishes picks, and hosts the picks itself. Whatever the record does, the action arrives. There has never been a cleaner illustration of the first rule of betting media — the picks are not the product. The handle is.
Which is the argument for keeping the receipts somewhere the house doesn't own.

sections.title: The Call
sections.headline: One Bet Left
paras: The card is not finished. Florida State, catching three against SMU, kicks off Monday night in Tallahassee — the only pick still live and the only chance to close the week above two wins. The market, for what it is worth, has drifted toward SMU by two and a half.

A fade of a man having this kind of week is not analysis; it is arithmetic. Then again, so was Furman plus forty-six and a half. That tension has a name, and it is the reason this desk exists. The Week 2 card is already up — he likes Texas over Ohio State, Oklahoma over Michigan, Clemson big over Troy — and when the next one drops it will be in Fade the moment it is posted, with a Tail button for the brave and a Fade button for the rest of us.

call.title: Florida State
call.note: He is 2–8 on the week and down 6.2 units. Monday night in Tallahassee is the last entry on the card — the only one still live, and the only chance to close Volume One above water.

body: Every autumn it happens on schedule: Clay Travis publishes his college football card for the world to see, and a measurable share of the internet does the profitable thing — the exact opposite. This is his fifteenth consecutive season of public picks. Week 1 of 2026: eleven picks, eight losses, a card 6.2 units underwater with only Florida State +3 still alive Monday night.

The margins were not close. His four long underdogs lost by 39, 52, 47 and 40 points. Furman +46.5 lost by exactly forty-seven — a cover dead by half a point. Georgia Tech, laying 6.5, lost outright on a touchdown with 42 seconds left and a blocked field goal at the gun.

None of this is new. By his own running count, 2024 went from 54–71 to 92–111 by title night. In 2017 and again in 2024 and 2025, fan blogs spent entire seasons mechanically betting the opposite of every pick he posted. All three fades finished profitable.
He said it himself, in November 2024: 'My college football picks have been such a disaster this year, you may be better off fading all my picks this week. But here they are.'

articles.title: The Drake Curse
articles.dek: Eighty-eight bets. Forty million dollars staked. Three million down. The most public betting ledger on earth, graded — Case File No. 001 reopens with the full record.

Individual bets and quotes as reported by Rolling Stone, UPI, CBS Sports, ESPN, Billboard, Complex, Fox, RTÉ and others. Stake deal value per Financial Times reporting, unconfirmed by either party. mag.coverSub: Iceman is ice cold when it comes to picking the right side.

quote.text: I am a flawed sports better. I will not deny that. That's not my gift.

sections.title: The Curse
sections.headline: First, the Folklore
sections.sub: A decade of losses he never bet on
paras: Before there was a ledger, there was a superstition. It grew up around Kentucky basketball in 2013, when Drake attached himself to a Calipari program that kept reaching Final Fours and never winning one. It went mainstream at the 2015 US Open, when he sat courtside as Serena Williams — two wins from the calendar Grand Slam — lost to Roberta Vinci in the semifinal. Serena, asked about it the next year, refused the premise: 'I'm the one who's playing, who's making mistakes or making winners. I'm not one to blame anyone else for anything.'

The internet was less rigorous. By 2019 the curse was a beat of its own: a PSG defender posted a photo with him and lost 5–1 the next day; AS Roma's official account jokingly banned its players from pictures with him until season's end; Anthony Joshua tweeted a photo captioned 'Bout to break the curse' and promptly suffered the biggest upset in modern heavyweight history. The night he walked Conor McGregor to the cage at UFC 229 — no bet, just an Irish flag — Khabib mauled him. The Raptors' 2019 title, with Drake courtside in a Dell Curry jersey, was supposed to be the exorcism.
Then, in February 2022, the folklore got a bankroll. He signed with the crypto sportsbook Stake and started posting the slips.

sections.title: The Ledger
sections.headline: Forty Million Dollars, Graded
paras: The independent tracker thedrakecurse.com has collected every publicly posted or reported bet since his first — $1.26 million in Bitcoin on Super Bowl LVI, February 13, 2022 — converting the crypto to dollars at the day of the wager. The file, as of its July update: 88 bets, $40.2 million staked, $37.2 million returned. Thirty-two wins, fifty-six losses. A 36.4 percent strike rate at an average stake of four hundred fifty-seven thousand dollars.

The arc is the story. He survived a seven-bet, $3.8 million losing streak in the fall of 2022 and still closed the year up $307,000. Then came 2023 — Jon Jones by submission at +580, Adesanya by knockout at +360, a million on Gervonta Davis — and by July he sat at plus $4.58 million, the high-water mark. He has been giving it back ever since: down $1.59 million in 2024, down $1.78 million in 2025, and down $3.27 million through July of this year, when the file hit its all-time low.

Here is the part the memes get wrong: the curse is mostly a myth. Of his fifty-six losses, the tracker counts only eleven 'actual curses' — favorites he backed that fell. Israel Adesanya accounts for three of them by himself. The rest of the file is something more ordinary and more expensive: long-odds moneylines at enormous stakes. The favorites don't die because he bets them. The dogs just don't come in.

figures.label: The running total
figures.caption: Cumulative profit and loss on publicly posted bets, in millions, February 2022 through July 19, 2026, per thedrakecurse.com. The peak came on July 8, 2023; the all-time low arrived with the World Cup final.

figures.label: The file, by sport
figures.note: His best sport, by return, is cricket — three bets, three wins. His worst is the one he keeps betting the World Cup on.

sections.title: The Exhibits
sections.headline: The Canon
sections.sub: The slips the file will be remembered for
paras: The wins are real, and they are spectacular: a three-hundred-nine-thousand-dollar, three-leg Game 7 parlay in May 2022 that returned $2.67 million; Jon Jones by submission at nearly six to one; $1.15 million on the Chiefs in Super Bowl LVIII, posted with the caption "I can't bet against the Swifties," which cashed for $1.2 million.

The losses are the genre's masterpieces. He bet $1 million on Argentina to win the 2022 World Cup final in ninety minutes; Argentina won the World Cup, on penalties, and the ticket died at 3–3. Four years later he bet $1.5 million on Argentina to win the 2026 final inside ninety — it was 0–0 at the whistle, and Spain won in extra time. The same bet, the same beat, two World Cups apart. In between: $1.6 million on Adesanya the night Pereira took his belt, a million on the Maple Leafs in a Game 7 they lost by five, and a million on Conor McGregor's comeback, which lasted sixty-nine seconds.
This summer, for balance, he also bet one dollar on Morocco. It won him forty-one cents.

sections.title: Not Like Us
sections.headline: The Kendrick Chapter
paras: On April 30, 2024, Kendrick Lamar released 'Euphoria,' and the most famous feud in rap history began grading Drake's slips in real time. On 'Meet the Grahams' the accusation was explicit: 'You got gamblin' problems, drinkin' problems, pill-poppin' and spendin' problems.' Drake's response was sarcasm — but the tracker's response was arithmetic: since the day 'Euphoria' dropped, it counts $7.2 million in betting losses.

The era produced the file's cruelest footnote. In July 2024 he put $300,000 on Canada to upset Argentina in the Copa América semifinal. Argentina won 2–0, and the Argentine national team's official account posted four words: 'Not like us, not with us.'

By June 2025 he was publishing the damage himself — an Instagram story showing $124.5 million wagered and $8.2 million lost in a single month, captioned 'Gotta share the other side of gambling.' Whatever the beef settled, the ledger's verdict arrived on its own schedule.

sections.title: The House
sections.headline: The Slips Are the Ad
paras: Every one of those posted slips is a screenshot from Stake, the crypto casino that signed him in 2022 in a deal the Financial Times has reported at roughly $100 million a year — a figure neither side has ever confirmed. The bets are content; the content is marketing. When he swore off sports betting after February's million-dollar Patriots loss — 'sticking to what I know' — he was back with three more seven-figure wagers by July.

The relationship is stormier than the feed suggests. In August 2025 he announced a gambling break, accused Stake of blocking his withdrawals and called its co-founder a snake on a livestream; by October he was betting there again. And in October 2025 a Missouri class action named Drake, Adin Ross and Stake, alleging among other things that the company fronts its stars house money — that the famous losses are, in effect, advertising. Stake disputes the suits, and called a Bloomberg analysis of its streamers' unusual slot luck 'categorically incorrect.' The courts will grade those claims; this desk only grades the slips.
Either way, the conclusion is the same one printed on the cover: whether the money is his or the house's, the record is public, and the record is 32–56.

call.title: Fade him.
call.note: Down $3.06 million all-time, $7.2 million since 'Euphoria.' By his own testimony: 'My slips do not cash out. But one day I'm gonna have a parlay that's insane.' Until that day, the file stays open.

body: Before the bets, there was folklore: Serena at the 2015 US Open, McGregor at UFC 229, a Roma squad jokingly banned from photos with him. Then, in February 2022, the folklore got a bankroll.

The independent tracker thedrakecurse.com has graded every publicly posted bet since: 88 bets, $40.2 million staked, a 32–56 record, down $3.06 million all-time — including a peak of +$4.58 million in July 2023 that took three years to give back.
Since Kendrick Lamar's 'Euphoria' dropped in April 2024, the tracker counts $7.2 million in losses. After the Copa América, Argentina's own team account posted: 'Not like us, not with us.'
His own verdict, from a mock press conference in May 2025: 'I am a flawed sports better. I will not deny that. That's not my gift.'

sections.title: The Record
sections.headline: Nine and Twenty-One
paras: Across thirty publicly reported wagers, Dave Portnoy's record is nine wins and twenty-one losses — a thirty percent hit rate. He is also up two million seven hundred thousand dollars. Both facts are true, and both facts are why America watches every slip he posts.

The losses are operatic. Half a million on Virginia Tech as a plus-220 underdog. A million on a Bills Super Bowl that never came. A thousand-dollar side bet with Urban Meyer that found a way to lose. But the wins are all-timers: six hundred thousand on Connecticut at 4-to-1 to repeat as national champion, three hundred thousand on Scottie Scheffler at 9-to-2 the week he won the Masters, a Caitlin Clark triple-double at 13-to-1.

sections.title: The Hedge
sections.headline: Two Sides of One Trade
sections.sub: Why the losses do not matter
paras: Jim McIngvale bets like nobody else on earth: nine-figure furniture promotions hedged with the largest sportsbook wagers ever written. The tracked record reads three wins and seventeen losses across roughly eighty-six million dollars in reported stakes — and he is up twenty-three and a half million. That is not a typo. It is a hedge.

Every giant ticket backs a 'win your mattress free' promotion at his Gallery Furniture stores. If the team loses, the promotion money stays home and the ticket is the cost of the marketing. If the team wins, the sportsbooks fund the refunds. The sportsbook money and the store money are two sides of one trade — which is why a 3–17 record can be a triumph.

figure.note: The 2022 Astros ticket paid $72.6 million — the largest payout in U.S. legal betting history.

sections.title: The Verdict
sections.headline: Stamped Tail, on Structure
sections.sub: The rare file where the record misleads
paras: He is the rare case stamped TAIL — not because the record is pretty, but because the structure wins regardless of it. The crown jewel: ten million dollars across five books on the 2022 Astros at long prices, paid out at seventy-two million six hundred thousand when Houston won the World Series. The scar tissue is real too — thirteen million gone on the 2019 Astros, nine and a half on the Bengals, three point three on the Patriots in Super Bowl LX.
Knowing the difference between a bad record and a bad bet is the whole game. This file is the proof.

call.title: Tail the structure.

sections.title: The Fade God
sections.headline: A Losing Streak, Monetized
paras: There are bad bettors, and then there is Trent Attyah — the first man to look at a losing streak and see a business model.

It began in 2021, when a run of losses went so publicly, spectacularly wrong that the internet started betting the opposite of everything he posted. Most people would have logged off. Attyah leaned in. He named the phenomenon, branded it, and built BookIt Sports around it. The Fade God was born — a career constructed entirely out of being wrong where everyone could see it.

The surgical streams are the masterpiece: followers submit picks live on air and Attyah assembles the day's parlay from the best of them, more than two hundred sixty thousand people watching every slip. Every pick is content. Every fade cashes twice — once at the book, once in the culture.
